strengths: Addresses a clear resource gap by constructing a 70k-scale paired corpus spanning CUDA/HIP source and NVIDIA SASS/AMD RDNA3 assembly across host and device code, with scraped, synthetic, and OpenCL components.

Substantial engineering effort is evident in the end-to-end pipeline: repository scraping, variable-persona LLM synthesis, HIPIFY conversion, dual-vendor compilation, host/device assembly extraction, filtering, and Docker-based generation.

The work is relevant to code intelligence and LLM research, targeting a low-resource cross-language/cross-architecture transpilation setting and releasing data, models, benchmark tasks, and tooling through Hugging Face and GitHub.

CASS-Bench uses execution-based evaluation and compares traditional tools, proprietary LLMs, an open coding model, and 1.5B/3B/7B fine-tuned variants. The paper also provides ablations, runtime/memory profiling, hardware details, training hyperparameters, and extensive synthetic prompt templates.

The results are suggestive: domain-specific fine-tuning enables smaller Qwen-based models to outperform zero-shot proprietary LLMs on the proposed benchmark, especially for source-to-source translation.
weaknesses: The central claim that the 70k pairs are functionally verified is overstated. The main pipeline primarily requires HIPIFY conversion and successful compilation on both stacks; most scraped or synthetic files lack independent test oracles. Compilation alone does not establish semantic equivalence, and only the 40 CASS-Bench cases are described as manually output-verified.

The assembly contribution needs stronger validation. SASS and RDNA3 outputs are generated independently from equivalent source rather than aligned instruction-by-instruction, so claims of instruction-level alignment are unsupported. The regex-based host/device extraction also lacks reported precision/recall or manual error analysis.

The CUDA assembly analysis raises contamination concerns: it reports x86-64 instructions such as movq, call, jmp, and pushq as dominant CUDA opcodes, whereas these are host instructions rather than NVIDIA SASS opcodes. The authors should clarify whether Figure 9 aggregates host and device code and demonstrate that the released SASS files are genuine device assembly.

The hardware/execution description is inconsistent. Appendix A.2 says CUDA work was performed on an A100 but targeted the sm85/RTX 4090 architecture, while the limitations section names an RTX 4090. An A100 cannot execute sm85 SASS, so it is unclear which artifacts were actually run, on which GPU, and whether the 70k dataset was execution-tested or only compilation-tested.

The evaluation is small and underpowered. CASS-Bench has only 40 tasks, with 1–5 tasks per domain. Thus 95% versus 90% source accuracy differs by only two cases and 37.5% versus 25% assembly accuracy by five cases; no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided.

The evaluation metrics are underspecified. The paper should define whether accuracy means exact textual match, successful assembly/linking, or differential execution; describe the assembly integration/linking harness and output normalization; and state the denominator used for the claim that 85% of translated assemblies preserve runtime and memory.
The abstract implies bidirectional CUDA↔HIP and SASS↔RDNA3 translation, but the experiments only support Nvidia-to-AMD directional generation. No reverse-translation models or results are reported.

Benchmark external validity is limited. The tasks are synthetic Claude-generated prompts, the AMD reference is regenerated until outputs match, and there is no held-out benchmark of real-world repository kernels. The domains also overlap the synthetic training templates, with no explicit contamination analysis.

The dataset is biased toward easier cases: files that HIPIFY can convert and that compile successfully under both toolchains are retained, while 43.9% of HIPIFY conversions and many generated files are discarded. Compiling with -Os to reduce token length further limits conclusions for production-optimized GPU code.

Performance claims are ambiguous and potentially confounded by different GPUs, host CPUs, compilers, and optimization levels. If the comparison is predicted RDNA3 versus reference RDNA3 on the same AMD GPU, this should be stated explicitly; t-SNE visualizations alone do not establish semantic opcode alignment.

Reproducibility would benefit from dataset splits, deduplication thresholds, filtering rules, the host/device extraction implementation, random seeds, training epochs/steps, counts of samples requiring context extrapolation, and exact baseline prompts, decoding settings, and model snapshots. The domain taxonomy is also inconsistently described as 16 domains versus seven keyword-matched categories.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-resourced problem: cross-vendor GPU portability from Nvidia/CUDA to AMD/HIP, including both source-level and low-level assembly translation.

The proposed CASS corpus is unusually broad in combining paired CUDA/HIP source with SASS/RDNA3 assembly, host and device artifacts, scraped code, synthetic kernels, and OpenCL samples. If the artifacts are complete, it could be a useful resource for code-intelligence and LLM-based transpilation research.

The data-construction pipeline is practically ambitious: it retrieves CUDA repositories, generates additional kernels, translates source with HIPIFY, compiles for both GPU stacks, and filters by successful compilation and execution.
The authors provide model-training details, scaling comparisons across 1.5B/3B/7B models, an ablation over data sources, and runtime/memory profiling rather than relying only on textual overlap.

The reported source-translation gains over zero-shot general-purpose LLMs and HIPIFY suggest that the corpus may help domain-adapt code models, although the strength of this conclusion is limited by the benchmark and evaluation concerns below.
weaknesses: The most central technical issue is that the assembly evaluation is under-specified. The paper states that generated host/device assembly is compiled and executed, but it does not explain how generated RDNA3 assembly is assembled, linked, or reinjected into the HIP binary, how kernel ABIs, registers, symbols, and relocation are handled, or whether assembly accuracy means exact match, compilation success, or functional pass rate.

The meaning of the reported 'accuracy' metrics remains unclear. The reader cannot determine whether source and assembly accuracy are exact-match, token-level, compilation success, pass@1, output equivalence, or another metric. This is essential for interpreting the 95% and 37.5% results.

CASS-Bench is very small for a benchmark claim: only 40 tasks across 16 domains, or 1–5 tasks per domain. At this size, one task changes accuracy by 2.5 percentage points, yet no confidence intervals, significance tests, or detailed failure analysis are provided.

The claim of semantic or instruction-level alignment between SASS and RDNA3 is overstated. Compiling functionally equivalent source programs yields whole-file or whole-kernel pairs, but it does not establish aligned instruction correspondences across two very different ISAs. The actual alignment granularity and extraction method need to be clarified.

The data and benchmark contain potential distribution bias. Most training labels are produced by HIPIFY, much of the synthetic data is generated by a Qwen2.5-Coder model from the same family used for fine-tuning, and CASS-Bench CUDA/HIP programs are generated by Claude-3.7 rather than drawn from independently written human AMD code. Decontamination and leakage checks are not reported.

The performance-preservation claim is ambiguous. The denominator for the 'over 85%' result is not clearly identified, and it is unclear whether it applies to all benchmark cases, only successfully compiled translations, or only source-level outputs. This must be reconciled with the much lower 37.5% assembly accuracy.

The baseline comparison is not entirely fair or well matched. ZLUDA is a runtime binary-interoperability system rather than an assembly-to-assembly translator, HIPIFY does not target assembly, and generic LLMs appear to be evaluated zero-shot on an extremely specialized output format. Prompting protocols, decoding parameters, and failure modes are insufficiently documented.

There are factual and numerical inconsistencies that undermine systems rigor. For example, an A100 is commonly compute capability sm80 rather than sm85, the hardware description later conflicts with the RTX 4090 mentioned in limitations, and 49.1% of 85k is approximately 41.7k, not the stated 46.3k valid files.

Generalization is limited because the dataset covers essentially one Nvidia ISA generation and one AMD RDNA3 configuration. The authors acknowledge this, but it further weakens broad claims about cross-architecture GPU translation.

Reproducibility would require substantially more detail on the regex-based host/device separation, assembly preprocessing, recompilation harness, test oracles, numerical tolerances, manual verification procedure, random seeds, decoding settings, and availability of the claimed GitHub/HuggingFace artifacts.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-resourced problem: cross-vendor GPU portability and low-level code translation between Nvidia CUDA/SASS and AMD HIP/RDNA3. The resource is relevant to code intelligence, compiler-aware LLMs, and software engineering.

Creates a comparatively large and multimodal paired corpus spanning CUDA/HIP source, host assembly, and device assembly, together with a 40-task execution-oriented benchmark across 16 GPU domains. This fills a gap relative to generic CUDA corpora such as The Stack and performance benchmarks that lack AMD-aligned assembly.

The data pipeline combines repository scraping, variable-augmented synthetic generation, HIPIFY translation, dual-vendor compilation, and filtering. The appendix provides substantial detail about synthetic prompt templates and placeholder values, which supports reuse and extension.

CASS-Bench is stronger than purely text-similarity evaluation because it emphasizes compilation, execution, and runtime/memory fidelity. Reporting both source-to-source and assembly-to-assembly outcomes, along with scaling and data-source ablations, gives useful insight into model behavior.

The fine-tuned CASS models show clear in-domain gains, especially for source translation: 95.0% for the 7B model versus 90.0% for GPT-4o and Claude-3.7. The 37.5% assembly result is still low in absolute terms but is nontrivial for a newly introduced task.

The planned release of data, models, benchmark code, and the construction pipeline has the potential to make this a useful community resource for future work on performance-aware and hardware-targeted code generation.
weaknesses: Several central claims are stronger than the documented evidence. The 70k corpus is aligned primarily by construction from equivalent source and successful compilation, but the paper does not describe test harnesses, inputs, or output checking for executing all 70k programs. “Execution-verified” should therefore be limited to CASS-Bench unless whole-dataset execution is demonstrated. The assemblies are also whole-program pairs rather than instruction- or basic-block-aligned pairs.

The CUDA↔HIP and SASS↔RDNA3 notation implies bidirectional support, but only Nvidia-to-AMD translation is evaluated. The paper should either report reverse-direction experiments or describe the pairs as one-way training/evaluation resources.

The assembly extraction pipeline needs stronger validation. The CUDA opcode analysis and word cloud are dominated by x86-64 host mnemonics such as movq, pushq, endbr64, and callq, raising concerns that supposed SASS device assembly may be contaminated with host code or that host and device artifacts are not consistently separated. Precision/recall of the regex-based filtering, device-only opcode statistics, and concrete SASS examples should be provided.

Assembly evaluation is under-specified. It is unclear how generated RDNA3 assembly is assembled, linked with host code, relocated, and executed; what counts as a failure; whether pass@1 or another metric is used; and what floating-point tolerances are applied. With only 40 benchmark tasks, 37.5% corresponds to only 15 successful programs, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

CASS-Bench is small and potentially biased. The CUDA and AMD reference implementations are generated with Claude-3.7, which is also evaluated as a baseline. References are regenerated until outputs match, while random-generator variance, seeds, numerical tolerances, and test inputs are not clearly specified. The benchmark would be more convincing with independent, human-written real-world programs and repository-level held-out tests.

Train/test contamination is not adequately controlled. The paper does not report repository-level train/validation/test splits, near-duplicate filtering across splits, or separation between synthetic training prompt templates and benchmark prompts. Since Qwen2.5-Coder is both the base model family and the synthetic data generator, and The Stack may appear in pretraining, contamination risk should be explicitly analyzed.

There are notable numerical and technical inconsistencies. For example, 24k Stack plus 46.3k compilable synthetic samples, followed by a reported 43.9% HIPIFY failure rate, is difficult to reconcile with the final 64k CUDA/HIP count. The hardware description is also inconsistent: an A100 is sm_80 and an RTX 4090 is sm_89, whereas the paper reports SASS sm_85.

Reproducibility would benefit from exact compiler and driver versions, CUDA/ROCm versions, complete compilation flags, Docker image digests, the modified ROCm patch used to defer binary injection, assembly extraction and reassembly scripts, baseline prompts and decoding parameters, random seeds, checkpoint-selection rules, and truncation rates for samples exceeding the 16K context.

The performance-fidelity claim needs a clearer denominator and protocol. It is unclear whether “over 85%” applies to all 40 source translations or only the approximately 15 successful assembly translations. Warmup procedures, hardware variability, synchronization, power/thermal controls, and statistical treatment of the 20 runs should also be specified.

The ablations are not fully controlled. Adding synthetic and OpenCL data changes both data composition and data volume, while RoPE extrapolation is an inference technique rather than a data type. Matched token budgets, training steps, random seeds, and repeated runs are needed before attributing gains specifically to each data source.

Domain labeling and coverage need clarification. The appendix describes seven keyword-matched high-level categories, while the main text claims 16 domains, and the synthetic prompts use yet another grouping. The simple keyword classifier has no reported validation, and many benchmark tasks are synthetic rather than drawn from production codebases.

The paper would be stronger with a more appropriate assembly baseline or upper-bound analysis, such as a rule-assisted translator, an IR-level baseline adapted to the benchmark, or a human/assembler success analysis. Zero-shot source-code LLMs scoring 0% on raw assembly is expected and does not by itself establish the difficulty of the task relative to alternative compiler-based approaches.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored code-intelligence problem: large-scale cross-vendor GPU transpilation at both source level (CUDA to HIP) and assembly level (SASS to RDNA3).

The 60k paired CASS dataset is a substantial resource, covering host and device code, real and synthetic programs, and 18 GPU-centric domains; it fills a clear gap relative to source-only or runtime-only GPU benchmarks.

The end-to-end pipeline is reasonably comprehensive: repository scraping, templated LLM synthesis, HIPIFY translation, compilation on both Nvidia and AMD stacks, assembly extraction, and execution-based filtering.
CASS-Bench uses a strict compile-plus-exact-output criterion and compares against a broad range of proprietary, open-source, reasoning, and coding-specialized models, plus ZLUDA and HIPIFY.

The model results are strong for a domain-specialized 7B system, particularly 69.11% strict assembly accuracy versus 22.22% for GPT-5.1, and the paper includes useful ablations for synthetic data, OpenCL, context extrapolation, and model scale.

The evaluation goes beyond text similarity by examining compilation, runtime, memory behavior, failure categories, qualitative errors, and cross-generation transfer from sm80 to sm89. The large degradation on sm89 is an important and honestly reported limitation.
The appendices provide substantial reproducibility support, including training hyperparameters, hardware, prompts, synthetic placeholder values, error taxonomies, and computational cost.
weaknesses: The labels are strongly shaped by HIPIFY and the two compiler stacks. Source references are HIPIFY outputs, while assembly references are only one possible RDNA3 compilation. Discarding HIPIFY failures also biases the dataset toward easily convertible programs and excludes important Tensor Core and matrix workloads.

The SASS-RDNA3 pairs are functionally aligned at the program or file level, not instruction-aligned. Because compiler, ABI, scheduling, and host integration differ substantially, assembly translation is inherently many-to-one; chrF against a single RDNA3 reference is therefore not a semantic metric.

Execution verification is under-specified. The paper does not clearly describe test-input generation, number of test cases, output oracles, floating-point tolerances, edge-case coverage, or human validation. Compilation and agreement on one output do not establish full semantic equivalence.

Data leakage is only controlled by exact deduplication. Training and benchmark examples can come from the same repositories, and synthetic programs generated from shared templates may be near-duplicates. Repository-held-out splits and near-duplicate detection are needed to justify generalization.

The claim that generated code matches native performance in 95% of cases is overstated. It appears to use absolute thresholds of about ±0.5 seconds and ±0.3 MB among successfully compiled samples, rather than relative runtime/memory overhead, confidence intervals, or statistical tests; failed translations are also excluded.

The source-level advantage over HIPIFY is only 88.17% versus 87.46%, so the abstract claim of outperforming HIPIFY by wide margins is not supported for source translation. Variances and significance tests for the main comparisons are not clearly reported.

Reproducibility would be stronger with an accessible artifact URL or DOI, dataset checksums, released model checkpoints, version-pinned containers, and explicit licensing terms. The regex-based Nvidia extraction and modified AMD compilation workflow may also be fragile across toolchain versions.

Practical portability remains limited: accuracy falls from 69.11% to 32.5% when moving from sm80 to sm89 SASS, and CASS-Bench contains 369 mostly kernel-scale tasks rather than full, previously unseen GPU applications. The keyword-based domain assignment is also a relatively coarse evaluation design.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem in cross-vendor GPU code portability, where little aligned CUDA/HIP or SASS/RDNA3 data previously existed.
Contributes a substantial engineered resource: approximately 60,694 paired source/assembly samples, a 369-task execution-oriented benchmark, synthetic data generation, and cross-compilation tooling.

The pipeline combines repository scraping, LLM-based synthesis, HIPIFY translation, NVIDIA/AMD compilation, host/device assembly extraction, and output matching, which is a non-trivial systems contribution.

Evaluation is broad in scope, covering 1.5B/3B/7B fine-tuned models, numerous open and closed models, source and assembly tasks, ablations, input-length effects, hardware transfer, compilation errors, and runtime/memory behavior.

The paper provides useful negative findings, especially the difficulty of SASS-to-RDNA3 translation for frontier general-purpose LLMs, severe sm80-to-sm89 degradation, and failure modes involving register banks and instruction constraints.

It includes many reproducibility details, such as training hyperparameters, hardware, Docker-based generation, prompts, placeholder values, energy measurements, and an intended open-source release of data, models, and tools.
weaknesses: The supervision is circular and subject to strong survivorship bias: HIPIFY generates the HIP labels and is the bridge into the AMD compilation branch, while files failing HIPIFY or either compiler are discarded. This excludes precisely the difficult Tensor Core, matrix, and low-level constructs that would make the benchmark representative. The paper does not sufficiently document test oracles, inputs, wrappers, floating-point tolerances, or human validation for the full 60,694 pairs, so calling them all semantically or functionally verified is not adequately supported.

The assembly pairs are whole compiler outputs rather than instruction-, basic-block-, or control-flow-aligned mappings. Pairing SASS and RDNA3 files from functionally related source does not establish fine-grained alignment, making the assembly translation task much noisier than implied. The regex-based host/device separation and the procedure for assembling, linking, and evaluating generated RDNA3 also need more complete documentation.

CASS-Bench is small and may be overly close to the training distribution: it contains only 369 tasks, is drawn from the same public-repository collection, and appears to use exact deduplication rather than repository-level or near-duplicate splits. Synthetic examples were generated by a Qwen2.5-Coder model and used to tune other Qwen2.5-Coder models, raising template- and family-distribution contamination concerns. The keyword-based domain labels are also not validated.

Several quantitative claims are overstated or statistically unsupported. The best source model beats HIPIFY by only 0.71 percentage points, roughly three tasks on a 369-task benchmark, with no paired significance test such as McNemar or bootstrap confidence interval; this should not be described as a wide margin. The claimed 22.2% advantage over GPT-5.1/Claude cannot be straightforwardly reconstructed from Table 3. Repeated-inference standard deviations do not substitute for benchmark-level uncertainty estimates.

The end-to-end metric uses exact output matching, but the paper does not explain how floating-point nondeterminism, numerical tolerances, or nondeterministic GPU reductions are handled. chrF similarity for assembly can also reward superficial token overlap without measuring valid or semantically equivalent code.

The claim that 95% of translations preserve native performance is not robustly established. It appears to condition on successfully translated samples and relies on absolute thresholds of about 0.5 seconds and 0.3 MB, rather than relative runtime/memory overhead, confidence intervals, warmup procedures, or paired statistical comparisons. A 0.5-second difference may be negligible for a long workload but very large for a short kernel.

Cross-hardware results substantially narrow the practical claim: accuracy falls from 69.11% on sm80-to-RDNA3 to 32.5% when the NVIDIA generation changes to sm89. The work should therefore be framed primarily as an sm80-to-RDNA3 proof of concept rather than a general NVIDIA-to-AMD solution.

The modeling contribution is standard instruction-supervised fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-Coder, with little new training or alignment methodology. The manuscript also contains inconsistent terminology and numerical claims, bidirectional arrows despite directional models, various typos, and no persistent artifact URL in the submitted version.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored code-intelligence problem: cross-vendor GPU transpilation at both source level (CUDA to HIP) and low-level assembly level (SASS to RDNA3).
Contributes a large-scale multilevel resource, CASS, with roughly 60k paired programs and an automated pipeline for scraping, synthesis, HIPIFY translation, compilation, filtering, and alignment.

CASS-Bench provides a useful execution-oriented evaluation with 369 tasks across 18 domains, strict train/test deduplication, compilation checks, and differential output comparison on both Nvidia and AMD hardware.

The empirical study is broad: it compares 1.5B/3B/7B domain-specialized models against numerous open and closed models, HIPIFY, and ZLUDA, and includes ablations, length analyses, hardware-transfer results, compilation-error analysis, and runtime/memory comparisons.

The fine-tuned models show a particularly large improvement on assembly translation, with the best model reaching 69.11% strict test accuracy versus 22.22% for GPT-5.1, demonstrating the value of in-domain aligned data.

The paper includes substantial reproducibility information, including hardware, training hyperparameters, prompts, synthetic-generation templates, Docker-based compilation, and energy measurements, and states that data, models, and tools will be open-sourced.
The work is relevant to NLP/code intelligence as a dataset, benchmark, and empirical study of code LLMs on a highly specialized and low-resource programming language translation task.
weaknesses: The verification status of the full 60k dataset is overstated. The construction pipeline primarily retains programs that compile successfully, while only CASS-Bench is explicitly described as executing successfully and passing differential tests. Compilation through HIPIFY does not by itself prove semantic equivalence, so the paper should distinguish compile-aligned training data from execution-verified benchmark pairs.

The claim that generated code matches native performance in 95% of cases needs qualification and stronger evidence. It appears to be conditional on successfully translated programs, uses absolute thresholds of about ±0.5 seconds and ±0.3 MB rather than relative slowdowns, and lacks clear reporting of denominators, confidence intervals, and workload-dependent variance.

Several evaluation details are underspecified. The paper should explain how predicted RDNA3 assembly is reassembled, linked, and executed; how benchmark inputs and drivers are produced; whether floating-point outputs require bitwise equality or numerical tolerance; and how many inference runs/seeds are used for stochastic models.

Although CASS-Bench spans 18 domains, some domains contain only one or a few tasks and the benchmark has only 369 programs overall. Domain coverage is therefore broad but sometimes shallow, and strict exact-output accuracy may be brittle on numerical kernels.

The source-translation advantage over HIPIFY is described with overly strong language. The best model achieves 88.17% versus HIPIFY's 87.46%, a difference of only 0.71 percentage point, equivalent to roughly 2–3 benchmark examples, with no significance analysis. The assembly margin is large, but the source margin is not.

The pairs are program-level equivalents produced from related source code rather than instruction-aligned mappings. Compiler-specific scheduling, register allocation, host/device separation, and regex-based assembly extraction may introduce label noise. Synthetic data generated by Qwen2.5-Coder and filtered only by compilation may also reflect generator bias, and additional near-duplicate/contamination analysis would strengthen the benchmark.

Cross-architecture generalization remains limited: accuracy falls from 69.11% to 32.5% when transferring from sm80 to sm89 Nvidia hardware. The dataset also has survivorship bias because only HIPIFY-convertible and successfully compilable programs are retained, excluding important Tensor Core and matrix-oriented workloads; the authors acknowledge this, but it narrows the central portability claim.

There is a reproducibility inconsistency in the hardware description: the dataset section refers to an A100 as using SASS sm85, while Table 3 correctly associates A100 with sm80 and RTX 4090 with sm89. The paper should also report how many training/benchmark examples are truncated under the 16K context window. Minor typographical and terminology issues should be corrected.

These concerns are mostly addressable through clarification, additional statistics, and qualified claims, and the core contribution appears publication-worthy; however, they currently prevent an unqualified main-conference recommendation.
